1191.event_title: Robert Schumann and Clara Wieck win the right to marry
1191.event: Clara Wieck's father, Friedrich Wieck, opposed her marriage to the composer Robert Schumann, rejected his written proposal and kept the couple apart. Robert and Clara took Wieck to court, and in 1840 the court ruled in their favour. They married on 12 September 1840 in the parish church at Schönefeld, near Leipzig.
1191.explanation: Because the love ran equally in both directions, the couple were willing to go to law together to win it, and their marriage became one of the great partnerships in music.
1191.tie_back: The kural calls love that is returned by the very one you love a seedless, all-sweet fruit, and the Schumanns fought for exactly that kind of matched love.
1191._accuracy_note: A strong, well-documented example of mutual love valued above all obstacles, though the kural's point is the sweetness of mutuality rather than the struggle to marry.

1192.event_title: Robert Browning's letters reach the invalid Elizabeth Barrett
1192.event: For years the poet Elizabeth Barrett lived as a chronic invalid, mostly confined to her room at 50 Wimpole Street. In January 1845 Robert Browning wrote to tell her he loved her verses with all his heart, and over the next twenty months the two exchanged 574 letters. They married secretly at St Marylebone Parish Church on 12 September 1846 and left for Italy, where her health improved and their son was born in 1849.
1192.explanation: Browning's love came into a shut-in, sickly life and helped open it up into marriage, travel, motherhood and her best-known love poetry.
1192.tie_back: The kural likens a lover's tenderness to rain for those whose life depends on it, and Browning's devotion arrived like that rain in Elizabeth Barrett's confined life.
1192._accuracy_note: Close fit to the image of life-giving tenderness; sources link her improved health partly to Italy's climate, so the rain-like effect of love should not be overstated.

1193.event_title: Sullivan Ballou's last letter to his wife Sarah
1193.place: Camp Clark, Washington, D.C., United States
1193.event: A week before the First Battle of Bull Run (First Manassas), Union Major Sullivan Ballou wrote a long letter to his wife Sarah, telling her of his love and of the possibility that he might not return. He was killed in the battle. The letter was never mailed; it was found among his belongings when Rhode Island's governor went to Virginia to recover the remains of the state's soldiers.
1193.explanation: The letter became one of the most famous love letters in American history because it speaks of a love so secure that even separation and death could not shake it.
1193.tie_back: The kural says only a woman truly loved can say with proud confidence that they will yet live happily even while he is away, and Ballou's letter is the kind of assurance that gives a wife that confidence.
1193._accuracy_note: The letter shows the husband's side of a secure, mutual love; Sarah's own feelings are not documented in these sources, and the letter reached her only after his death.

1194.event_title: Catherine of Aragon is set aside by Henry VIII
1194.event: In 1527 Henry VIII asked the pope to annul his long marriage to Catherine of Aragon, arguing that it broke a biblical rule. Catherine appealed to Rome and insisted she was his lawful wife; Britannica notes that she had always been loved by the English people. Henry separated from her in 1531, Archbishop Thomas Cranmer declared the marriage void on 23 May 1533, and she died at Kimbolton in January 1536, still signing herself queen.
1194.explanation: Catherine kept the affection and respect of the country, yet none of it could make up for the husband who had turned away from her.
1194.tie_back: The kural says a woman admired by everyone is still unfortunate if the one she loves does not love her back, which is the shape of Catherine's last years.
1194._accuracy_note: Strong fit: public admiration and a husband's rejection are both documented; her inner feelings are inferred from her conduct and her final letter, not stated in the event.

1195.event_title: Ivan Turgenev's lifelong devotion to Pauline Viardot
1195.place: St Petersburg, Russia; Paris, France; Baden-Baden, Germany
1195.event: The Russian writer Ivan Turgenev fell in love with the singer Pauline Viardot when she first performed in Russia in 1843. In 1847 he left Russia for Paris to be near her, and after the Crimean War he moved to Baden-Baden, again to be with her; he wrote the libretto for her operetta Le dernier sorcier (1869). He later settled at Bougival, near Paris, where he died in 1883.
1195.explanation: Turgenev organised his whole adult life around a woman who gave him friendship and artistic partnership but never married him.
1195.tie_back: The kural asks what good the beloved can do if he does not love in return, and Turgenev's decades of following Viardot show both how much such love asks and how little it can be sure of receiving.
1195._accuracy_note: Next-best fit: Turgenev's devotion is well documented, but how far Viardot returned his feelings is debated, so this is not a clear case of wholly unreturned love.

1196.event_title: Goethe falls in love with the engaged Charlotte Buff
1196.event: In May 1772 the young Goethe went to Wetzlar as a trainee at the Imperial Chamber Court. At a dance on 9 June he met Charlotte Buff, the fiancée of his friend Johann Christian Kestner, and fell in love with her; on 11 September he left the town. Within two years he turned the experience into his first novel, The Sorrows of Young Werther, in which the hero loves a Lotte who is engaged to another man, and the book became an immense success.
1196.explanation: Goethe's one-sided love was painful enough to drive him away, while Charlotte and her fiancé, whose love ran both ways, stayed together and became the models for Lotte and Albert.
1196.tie_back: The kural compares love to a carrying pole that is painful when loaded at one end and sweet when balanced at both, and Wetzlar showed both ends: Goethe's lopsided love and the engaged couple's balanced one.
1196._accuracy_note: Good illustration of one-sided love's pain beside a mutual couple, though the sweetness of the balanced side is implied rather than described in the sources.

1197.event_title: W. B. Yeats and his unreturned love for Maud Gonne
1197.event: The Irish poet W. B. Yeats met Maud Gonne in 1889 and later wrote that the troubling of his life began then. About two years later he proposed and she refused; he asked again in 1899 and she declined, admiring him but not returning his love, since her passion was for Ireland's cause. In 1903 she married Major John MacBride, and Yeats's unreturned love fed many of his greatest poems over some forty years.
1197.explanation: Yeats's case is a classic of love that took hold of one person completely while leaving the other untouched in the same way.
1197.tie_back: The kural complains that the god of love works on one side only, and in Yeats's story love struck the poet again and again while Maud Gonne stayed free of it.
1197._accuracy_note: Strong fit for one-sided love; the kural's speaker is a wife addressing the love god, while here the lover is a man who never married his beloved.

1198.event_title: Beethoven's letter to the Immortal Beloved
1198.event: In July 1812, at the spa town of Teplitz, Beethoven wrote a passionate ten-page letter in pencil to a woman he addressed only as his Immortal Beloved. The letter was apparently never sent; it was found among his belongings after his death on 26 March 1827, and scholars still do not know for certain who it was meant for. Beethoven never married.
1198.explanation: The letter shows a great love that, as far as the record shows, never became a shared life, and Beethoven went on working for fifteen more years without it.
1198.tie_back: The kural calls those who go on living without a sweet word from their beloved the hardest, or bravest, of all, and Beethoven's unsent letter points to that kind of endurance.
1198._accuracy_note: Next-best fit: we do not know how the woman felt or whether she ever sent him kind words, so the link to living without a sweet word is an inference from the unsent letter and his single life.

1199.event_title: Dante writes La Vita Nuova in praise of Beatrice
1199.event: Dante first saw Beatrice, usually identified as Beatrice Portinari, when he was nine, and he saw her only rarely after that. She married Simone de' Bardi and died in 1290 at about twenty-four. Around 1293 Dante wrote La Vita Nuova, prose and poems tracing his devotion to her, and ended it with a vow to write of her as no woman had been written of before, a vow he fulfilled in the Divine Comedy.
1199.explanation: Dante received almost nothing from Beatrice in life, yet speaking and writing of her became the centre of his poetry.
1199.tie_back: The kural says that even if the beloved shows no kindness, every word about them is sweet to hear, and Dante filled whole books with words about a woman who gave him little more than a few meetings.
1199._accuracy_note: Good fit for love that delights in the beloved's name and praise without return; Beatrice's own feelings are unknown, and some details of her identity rest on early commentators.

1200.event: In a note on the flyleaf of his copy of Virgil, Petrarch recorded that he first saw Laura on 6 April 1327 in Avignon and that she died on 6 April 1348. Over some twenty years of work he collected his Italian love lyrics in the Canzoniere, with 263 poems on Laura in life and 103 after her death; in them she offers him little encouragement. Her real identity and feelings remain uncertain.
1200.explanation: Petrarch kept pouring his longing into poem after poem addressed to a woman who, in his own account, did not answer it, and in doing so shaped European love poetry for centuries.
1200.tie_back: The kural tells the heart that telling its pain to one who does not care is like trying to fill the sea, and Petrarch's hundreds of poems to an unresponsive Laura are that endless pouring.
1200._accuracy_note: Strong match to the image of endless complaint to an unresponsive beloved; scholars debate whether Laura was a real woman, though Petrarch's note and poems are certain.
